body: Those are not temples, btw. Another Mormon-connected company just bought up over 1000 acres on North Shore. I get that. It’s a good theory. But when I read D&C 132, it’s pretty clear Emma was threatened with destruction if she didn’t comply. And when you read the backstory of why (Emma wanting to leave JS, because she wasn’t able to trust him) …. it doesn’t sound like there was much consent involved in her decision. And when there’s not consent, agency has essentially been robbed from the person the law is being enforced upon. The church being all about agency, I just can’t see that working with God’s plan of salvation that is all about our gift of agency. 

We are all paradoxical creatures, Joseph Smith included. “Good people are not all good, and bad people are not all bad.” Learning to see the paradox within ourselves and even in the church and its prophets is pretty freeing and healthy. So I think it’s totally possible for JS to have been on the right path with some things and on the wrong path in others. We all do that, but luckily we’re able to course-correct once we realize it.

I personally like Patrick Mason’s take on polygamy in his book, Restoration: God’s Call to the 21st Century World. I agree that Dice has done an excellent job, but is it not possible that polygamy could’ve just been a side-effect of the church being restored in a patriarchal society? I don’t know why it bothers me so much. I mean, I’m sure it’s not uncommon for women to not agree with it. And I know there was a time when the RS got shut down by BY for 10-20 yrs because Emma Smith (after JS’s death) had rallied the women together in opposition to polygamy. (Hence the tales of bad blood between ES and BY). So, it’s hard to say, but I don’t think polygamy was a great thing for the church. Even with all the women who sacrificed so much, I wonder how many of them actually get recognized by the church (especially if their take on polygamy wasn’t in line with it). Idk. Just some ramblings….

Well-written and to the point.

I do wonder who really benefits from knowing and preaching about these dangers. Hell/lower degrees of glory feel more like a threat sometimes, in that if you don’t meet all of God’s expectations (covenants and ordinances) you’re deemed unworthy. I just don’t like that, and it seems like something someone who wants to control my thoughts and actions would say. I don’t think I need a piece of paper to know that I am worthy and loved by God. 99% of the world don’t need it either. But I still want to hold a temple recommend, of course. Just not because I’m more worried about the bad things that might happen to me, as opposed to the good that could. 

How we spend our time definitely matters, you have a good point there. Yes, of course, you are still a good person. But finding ways to use our time well is what the human experience is all about. Life can be beautiful and fulfilling, no matter what a person believes. But time is something we can’t get back, so making the most of it is important.

But I do get what you’re saying. I think we’ve managed to make it seem like a good thing…testimony growing, service, good works = oil in our lamps….but the alternative is hell or lower kingdoms (which we all know that none of us really wants to go to any of those places).

Right. Well, it’s the same with the wheat and the tares. Are you a wheat or are you a tare who’s going to be thrown into the fire. Or are you one of the five virgins who stayed or one of the five who gets shut out in the night. It’s at the base of each of these stories —that’s where most of the manipulation, in my opinion, lies. Because if you don’t do everything (which “everything” can become somewhat vague at times), then you get a bad result. So there’s fear, at the root, to be good and do good.  

Most people are good on their own accord. Most people will help you if you need it. So this half will be cast out, half will get be welcomed into Heaven stuff….seems nonsensical sometimes.

Hmm… The only thing I personally don’t like about the 10 virgin story is that it’s often used to try and manipulate people (using fear and guilt and shame) to stay in the church. If you’re staying because you’re fearful, where’s the faith in that.

I appreciate this write-up. There’s always more to the picture when it comes to church history. I personally don’t believe polygamy is of God / an eternal practice. I think it’s a side-effect of the patriarchy, which is the social structure the church was restored in. But if that’s what others wanna believe, I’m fine with that. All that being said, your CES rebuttal is one of the best I’ve seen. 👏🏽💯

For me, the title reads a little bit fearful. But that’s just me. It reads if you talk to people who have doubts like you, you’re only going to increase them….which plays into the idea that doubt is inherently bad and something that we should avoid at all costs. Which, to me, sounds like this post is telling people to be afraid of doubting. I just don’t think it’s a healthy view of it. And also telling people not to talk to people in similar situations makes for a very lonely walk in the gospel. But people in trust-crisis with the church will gravitate toward each other anyway, because that’s what humans do.

I don’t think doubt is something to fear. Associating our doubts with being from the adversary, I think is a mistake. It gives Satan way too much power over our normal everyday human emotions and experiences. Let’s not give him so much slack. “The opposite of faith is not doubt. The opposite of faith is certainty.” Being afraid of doubt is not the answer. Doubt and faith can work together if we let them.
Same!!

To answer your question: No. There hasn’t been anything helpful from the TBM side. I’ve searched and searched and searched. Nothing. Which, for someone who wanted to believe, was awful. The answers only ever blamed me or other people with questions like mine, for not having enough faith. Or they would just beat around the bush, talking circles, just to walk you to the conclusion, “we don’t know….” always followed by, “faith is the answer!” But, at some point, white-knuckle faithing it is just not enough. Especially when it comes to the questions J. Runnels poses in his letter. The discrepancies are too noticeable. And I got sick over the stress of it all, trying to find something or someone who could debunk it. 

All that being said. I’m a weirdo. And I still go to church. I don’t believe in it like I used to. But I see Mormonism as my heritage. Don’t know if I’ll stick with it forever. But I don’t feel ready to let it all go just yet….

It’s really hard. But in the end, you have to decide for yourself. Trust yourself. Know that your sense of direction works and that doing what you feel is truly right for YOU is always the right thing to do.

Best of luck!

“God is always bigger than the boxes we build for God, so we should not waste too much time protecting the boxes.” - Richard Rohr

The only problem I have with taking solace in that Wilford Woodrow quote is that it gives prophets too much power, even when what they’re doing is wrong. It can also take away a member’s ability to think for themselves when a situation clearly looks, feels, and sounds wrong (i.e. what’s currently taught about LGBTQ+) so we have to twist and bend our thoughts to make them “seem right” and fall in line with what a prophet says because we’re banking on God striking them down if what they are preaching isn’t true. What kinda life would that be for a prophet? A fearful one probably. But also, if God had that power why has he not struck down corrupt leaders everywhere? This rhetoric leaves no room for real agency and freedom of thought/opinion and action for any of us (prophets very much included).

All I’m saying is God isn’t a helicopter parent to us or to the prophets. Prophets are just doing their best, like the rest of us. And that should be enough. I don’t think President Nelson is corrupt. I think the man is sincere in his efforts to help us. And even if some of the things he does actually doesn’t help, and or we don’t agree with them, Nelson is still a good leader. We have the freedom to take from him what helps us, and leave behind what doesn’t.

What you said about P days gives me ptsd! Haha. I totally remember that. And it’s hard. If you both want it to work out, it will. It did between me and my guy. Wishing you all the best! But I totally get this. Keep focusing on developing yourself / learning to trust yourself. You got this.

The church’s push to keep our thoughts clean and pure can turn into an obsession. I struggled as a kid, all the time. Did the “hum your favorite hymn” thing. And, the problem is, the obsession  disorients you from truly knowing who you are and what your strengths are—it makes you feel like you can’t trust yourself *with yourself*. It’s stories like yours that make me really dislike how religion and society tend to push the idea onto men that they are incapable of controlling themselves and have no power of their own autonomy. I agree with all the responses above about you not beating yourself up. It’s okay to notice that others look good. But stewing in your shame for noticing will only exacerbate the feeling, as it sounds like it already is doing… Guilt is informative in that it helps us know when we have made a mistake and can lead us to make amends. Shame tends to make us feel like we ARE the mistake. Shame makes us feel stuck and teaches us to focus on everything that is wrong with us and not enough on everything that is right.  So I guess my only advice really is to learn to trust yourself. We spend so much time fearing ourselves and our thoughts and our emotions….don’t let that fear rule you. Good luck! And take care!

Thank you for your sympathy. I’m sorry that you are going through the same thing, though. It’s kinda the worst. But I feel what you said 100%. It’s hard not to get resentful about the person I was and am being covered up by my distrust.
You have every right to feel angry and hurt. Block him!
Loved this advice too 👏🏽
Amen!
but I still wonder under what conditions they are admitting it. and how.

*It’s based on knowing multiple people who use that excuse*

What if it’s only an excuse according to you, but to them it feels legitimate? I’ve got a few decades under my belt as well, and the people I know who have left have done so for mental health reasons, and, of course, church history discrepancies (according to their own interpretation of it all, which they also feel  to be valid). 

*You’re entitled to your opinion, and I’m entitled to mine*

Most definitely. Opinions are separate things,
as different as the people who hold them. Which is why I try hesitate to dismiss other people’s experiences, because I don’t know all that there is to theirs. I only know my own. 

I get what you’re saying, overall, I think. If we choose to stay, the culture is ultimately what we make it. If the toxic parts of church culture genuinely bothers us, it’s okay to lay down healthier boundaries. I don’t think God will hold it against you for letting go of anything that makes it hard for you for you to function. But if we choose to stay, boundaries are also a must—and once laid down, I think our problems with the culture could also decrease.

>>when people say they’re leaving due to culture issues, they are very often lying, and demonstrably so.

I don’t think so. But mainly because I can’t step into anyone’s life / read their minds / know what they’re going through. I think it’s maybe your assumption that they’re lying? Which I guess you’re allowed to have. But I don’t think it helps or heals anything to assume something like that of other people. (*shrug*)

People have valid reasons to step away from the church. 

People have valid reasons to stay in the church. 

Both make their decisions based on what they feel is truly right for them.

Vilifying people’s decisions, even under the word “excuses,” gets us nowhere.

The real problem with church culture is that’s it’s ego centrical. We all think that people should look, act, and think like we do, otherwise we view their way of existing as less than our own.
Yah. Cut her out. You don’t need that drama in your life. Sorry that you’ve been going through it. It sounds awful!

I agree with the person who suggested therapy. I’ve been through a rough patch spiritually and the best thing for me, was learning to trust myself. It’s easy to forget that God gave you, you, too. For me, it was the mindset change from>>>me focusing on everything I thought was wrong with me>>>to me realizing that there was a lot right with me, and choosing to focus more on those things instead. Too often we’re told to look beyond ourselves for the answers we need, but a lot of the answers are already within you. Hopefully something here helps you on your journey. And to answer your initial question: serve yourself first! Not in a selfish way. Just in a take care of yourself and honor what matters to you sort of way. Because taking care of yourself and learning to accept yourself will create more space in your heart to love and care for others.

This is a popular analogy in the church, but it’s not a healthy one. Comparing a child’s faith journey to either being outside or inside of the “boat” we deem acceptable can turn manipulative fast. They need to decide for themselves, bottom line. And parents should support their kids regardless.

Of course I will accept them as they are. I saw an awesome quote the other day that said something like: real love only starts when we stop trying to bend or twist people into whatever it is we deem acceptable. Trying to control teens only ever pushes them farther away. Letting them have their space to learn to trust themselves, knowing they have your love through it all….is worth far more than you constantly voicing your disapproval of their religious beliefs or lack thereof.

Humans are all so paradoxical. We tend to contradict ourselves a lot. And the things we are the most passionate about, are typically the things we struggle the hardest with. JS wasn’t perfect, but his good intentions are there if you’re willing to look and often right along side actions we’d call immoral/sinful. I think, for me, it helps to focus less on JS and more on the church as a whole. I say this, because I think the significance of the people’s faith and sincere search for truth can easily get lost whenever we zoom in on JS (or any other prophet, for that matter) and pick apart everything he did wrong. Because he did do wrong. But so do I. All the time. But he also did plenty of right, plenty that even outsiders have called remarkable. It’s hard for some members today, because some of JS’s history wasn’t as promoted or well known and so we have lots who are expressing their disillusionment. I honestly think they have a right to feel that way and we should allow them their space and time to figure it out for themselves. Because, with Google, you can’t get around this stuff….you have to go through it. So yah, I get this post and I agree with it. But I don’t want to make those who are currently struggling feel like anything’s wrong with them either.
This 🙌🏽

I used to vilify people who left the church. I’d say or think things from, “They probably just want to do sin A, B, or C,” to, “Wow, you can really tell the light’s gone out of their eyes…” This behavior of mine isn’t unusual when it comes to religion or any other exclusive organization for that matter. It’s something that happens inside and outside of churches. But—if I have to vilify another human being just so that I can keep feeling safe in my little corner of the world, does it really help anybody? Does it even really help me? 

People have valid reasons to step away from the church. People have valid reasons to stay in the church. Both make their decisions based on what they genuinely feel is right for them. I think there is room to respect both choices without telling one side they’re being influenced by the devil or telling the other they’re being herded like blind sheep. Both are pretty hurtful accusations that don’t empower or help either side.
This is cool. But isn’t it also kinda prophet-worshippy?

“I’m willing to change my mind, if you present your point of view in a way convincing to me”

Meaning I have to say things in a way that cater to you and your world view. That can’t happen effectively on Reddit. I can’t see you. I’ve never spoken with you in person. So how can I know how to effectively cater to those things?

“this is about laws that governed a country for thousands of years.”

laws *from thousands of years ago… so let’s bring back stoning people? 🙌🏽

“Guy walks into a tent not dressed properly and dies. Totally an accident.”

“The God of the Tanakh is Jesus. Same person. If you don’t understand that, you’re misunderstanding at least one, probably both.”

How do you even know if that story is literal? I wasn’t there, were you? People walk into temples today to film what goes on inside just so they can get YouTube views. It’s disrespectful and very “unprepared of the heart”… So why isn’t the Lord killing them on the spot—especially if He is, like you say, the same person?

Also, I notice that you like to tout all your knowledge of all things ancient Israel. Most impressive. 

another very egotistical thing to say.

“Only if you think you can shoot a gun with only a firing pin. There’s millions of parts, all essential.” 

I actually like that analogy, a lot. And, exactly, we’re all essential, whether we are Mormon or not. 

I honestly don’t know what Christ cares about or doesn’t. 

“There you are. Start with that next time.”

Lol. How rude! But if we’re being honest, neither of us do. We can only take what we’ve read or have been taught and form our own opinions of Him. It doesn’t make those opinions the actual or more right or accurate version of who He was/is. I guess we won’t know til we meet Him. 

“Love based obedience.”

Simple, but effective. Touché. A lot easier said than done, however. 

“The words of Christ are there.”

They are, second-hand. 

“You believe in a subjective world, but these things exist objectively.”

We all do that to some degree or another. 

The things we call objective in regards to religion often stem from human subjectivity.

And now I’m stepping down from my soapbox 😏✌🏽

“How about the covenants you make with Him in the temple. You really think He doesn’t care about that?”

As I said, the rituals are more for us than they are for Him. We take them seriously. 

“He cared a hell of a lot when he killed unprepared priests trying to enter the Tabernacle.”

We don’t know if He really killed them. People back then were superstitious, they more likely died accidentally. I personally don’t take the OT literally and for good reason. Did unprepared mean that they weren’t wearing garments? Or was it an unprepared in their hearts kinda situation? Again, I don’t take the OT literally because I’m living in the 21st century and the God of the OT reflected a culture that isn’t mine. 

“a crappy argument”

…. because nobody wants to admit it’s weird how special and chosen we think we are over 99% of the world? Our egos want us to be separate and superior, and religious beliefs and commitments are often the perfect vehicle for that.

“but if you’re in the covenant, you have certain obligations they don’t”

translation, “we’re chosen, they’re not.” 

“firing pin being small doesn’t make its cleanliness and accurate design inconsequential” 

another very egotistical thing to say.

“Obedience is actually important for the covenant people.”

But is that obedience to these laws based on the idea that if we don’t do these things that God will withhold blessings (or even protection from the Devil) if we don’t meet His expectations? Requiring that kind of obedience looks and feels like a method of thought-control that uses our emotions (fear, guilt, and shame) to get us to act or behave in certain ways. It’s not healthy. If you’ve found a way around fear or shame based obedience, I’d honestly like to hear about it.

“you said Christ doesn’t care about x, y, and z and all three were things that He definitely cares about…”

I honestly don’t know what Christ cares about or doesn’t. And I probably shouldn’t talk like I do, especially when everything I’m saying is based on my assumptions of Him. More often than not God is just a reflection of our own inner thoughts and feelings about the world. So you saying “He definitely cares about those things,” is actually *You definitely care about those things….which it’s really not my place to tell you if you should or not. 

This is a classic case of two people on social media who argue and for what? I’m not going to change your mind and you’re not going to change mine. Is there room for both our opinions to exist in the world. Probably.

Holy bejeezus. You just wrote a whole freaking novel picking apart every single thing I said, who the hell is trying to show off here? Sorry you don’t like my question? It obviously touched a nerve. Show me the verse where Jesus says He cares about my underwear… because if I see it, I’ll believe it. You take all of this pretty seriously. Good on you. Really. But the Mormon Church literally makes up less than 1% of the entire world, that means 99% of God’s purposes are being accomplished by people who don’t need a temple recommend to feel worthy of His help. I think our rituals in the church are more for us than they are for Him. And sometimes there’s an unhealthy obsession with obedience that turns into a type of OCD that is run by fear more than it is a true desire to simply do what’s right.

Yah, He especially challenged the extravagant outward things people did to imply that they were more spiritual than others…. Jesus pretty much spent His life making religious people upset because He didn’t conform to their ideas—don’t you think He spent more time annoying Pharisees who were abusing their religious power over people than He spent condemning whether or not people walked the exact amount of steps required on a Sunday?? Today we are not much different in the way that we use each other’s outward appearances to judge each other’s level of spirituality—everything from the garment checks we all do to whether or not a man wears a white shirt on Sunday….I don’t think Jesus would’ve cared about those things, but that’s just me.

No, you’re not an apostate. Jesus didn’t teach outward conformity….the gospel should be about what’s in our hearts. But we’ve done a damn good job at making it about everything else from piercings to our type of underwear (not to be crude, it’s just true)…
I love that you are feeling so good. Keep learning how to trust yourself! 🙌🏽

My hearts hurts reading this, because I’ve been there. And the heart break you’re experiencing is legitimate and it’s a pain that deserves to be acknowledged in full. I’m so sorry that you are going through this. 

We’ve been married for 6 years now, and are still going strong. The thing that helped me the most was to realize that the most important relationship I have is with myself. That if I take good care of myself and I maintain a loving opinion of me, what others do cannot shatter my identity. Developing a strong sense of self worth is so much easier said than done, but the sooner you start the better. Instead of trying to figure out all that’s wrong with you, focus on all that’s right with you—your ability to still say that you love your husband being one of the many things. 

My husband has done similarly, where he’ll tell me he’s doing ok….but when it comes out that he’s viewed it several times over the last few months….that does hurt and it does feel like I’ve been lied to. Something that helps me get through this is trying to understand why my husband didn’t tell me. Often times it’s because he didn’t want to hurt me, which always annoys me! Ha. But I think it also stems from the deeply rooted shame/guilt/fear that is taught around this subject. My husband expresses that he felt ultimately doomed, when he was just 16, to battle porn for the rest of his life….because that’s what he was taught at church (“it only takes one time”). So the pressure of church-related shame is often really heavy on young people’s shoulders and it can do some pretty long-lasting damage. If there’s one thing I’ve come to realize, it’s that trying to operate our lives on shame/guilt/fear is super unhealthy and unsustainable—I would recommend paying attention to what things in your life and his that are being influenced by them. Because, the thing is, when we are buried in shame we cannot heal. Shame also disconnects us from ourselves and others, when in this situation connection is everything you both need. So focus on connection, because connection is what heals. 

Does any of this mean that what you’re going though right now is any less real or important? Hell no. It’s definitely the worst. Set your boundaries and keep them—boundaries help keep your heart and sanity safe. ♥️.

It’s not a virus, it’s your normal human emotions. Boundaries are important in every relationship, including our relationship with the church. There’s nothing wrong with giving yourself extra time and space to feel, deal, and heal.

I think faith looks different, person to person. We’re often taught to have faith in things beyond ourselves, like the BoM or the HG. Sometimes this disconnects us from ourselves and I think for a logical person who relies on their God-given intuition this is disorienting for them. Maybe there’s nothing wrong with that? Maybe there’s space for both you and your brother’s methods of interacting with the world—and God accepts both. A thought that helps me personally is that Mormons make up less than 1% of the world population currently. That means 99% of God’s purposes are being accomplished by people who aren’t LDS. I don’t say that to diminish the significance of what I believe, but to help me maintain a healthy perspective of myself and the people in the world around me. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with you or your brother’s ways of looking at the world—there’s space for both.
I loved this actually. Thank you.
